keep: The bonds that finished him stood for a deal he never made. The auditors traced the rest back to 1917.
lede: The Italian bonds that finished him stood for a loan he never made. His talks with Italy broke off in 1930; after his death the auditors found £21 million of its government bonds, fabricated.
copy: Ivar Kreuger was born in Kalmar on 2 March 1880, studied mechanical engineering in Stockholm, and spent seven years building abroad: in the United States, Mexico, Toronto and South Africa, where he also ran a restaurant. In 1908 he and Paul Toll founded Kreuger & Toll to build in reinforced concrete, then a new technique. On 4 November 1910 the firm signed to build the stadium for the Stockholm Olympics, estimated at 508,450 kronor; it went up in granite and brick. In 1913 he merged a group of match factories, in 1917 he formed Svenska Tändsticks AB, and in 1923 International Match Corporation in the United States. Kreuger & Toll came to involve more than four hundred subsidiaries in as many as 99 countries.

His trade was loans for monopolies. Between 1925 and 1930 the group lent nearly 1.3 billion kronor to sixteen states in nineteen loans, from $1 million to Danzig to $125 million to Germany, agreed in October 1929 and paid out after the crash. Every borrower but one granted a match monopoly in return. The exception was the largest early loan: France took $75 million in 1927 and gave no monopoly, after talks on one came to nothing. Where he did get them, state price controls held profits down, and some ran at a loss. The money came from investors. In 1929 Americans bought $50 million of Kreuger & Toll debentures, secured on collateral with a par value over $60 million. The collateral was substituted, and what replaced it was later worth about 20 cents on the dollar.

On 12 March 1932, in Paris, after the Swedish central bank's investigators had questioned him about the Italian bonds among other things, he killed himself. Price, Waterhouse & Co. began work eleven days later and filed 57 reports. The final one, of 28 November 1932, dated the manipulation of the accounts to 1917 at the latest. From 1918 to March 1932 the group reported earnings of 1,179 million kronor. It had earned 151 million. It paid outside holders 668 million in dividends and interest, and Kreuger withdrew a net 432 million for himself. The auditors found nothing to support "the view that Kreuger possessed business ability so extraordinary as to warrant the grant to him of the freedom from control or disclosure of his actions which he enjoyed." What he had really earned came to about 1½ per cent on the capital.

bio.t: The Match King: Ivar Kreuger, the Financial Genius Behind a Century of Wall Street Scandals
bio.why: The only modern life in English built from the financial instruments and the American record. It is sympathetic, and its claim that he shaped the Securities Acts is an argument, not a finding. Read the Svenskt biografiskt lexikon's article beside it, and the Price Waterhouse report, printed in full in the Senate hearings of January 1933.

contested: Whether he was a fraud from the start, whether he killed himself, and how much he changed American law. Price Waterhouse put the manipulation back to at least 1917, on a large scale from 1923 and 1924. Frank Partnoy's The Match King (2009) reads him as a real industrialist who overreached and then hid his losses. The Svenskt biografiskt lexikon, in an article by Jan Glete, Björn Gäfvert and Anders Hiller, sits between: he paid dividends partly out of capital, and probably expected later profits to make the reported ones true. That he was murdered has been argued since B. Heed and S. Stolpe's Ivar Kreuger mördad? (1955), by his brother Torsten among others, and by the journalist Jan Gillberg, who points out that no autopsy was done although the family asked for one. The lexikon notes that much of this defence was Torsten's effort to clear his own name after his own fraud conviction. Partnoy, and Flesher and Flesher in The Accounting Review (1986), argue that the collapse shaped the Securities Act of 1933; this house has not read the Fleshers' paper. The Senate heard the Kreuger case in January 1933, as part of its hearings on stock exchange practices, about four months before the Act. Two things often printed are not here. The $142 million usually given for the Italian bonds is not in the auditors' report, which says £21 million nominal. And the lines quoted from his last note are left out, because the house has not seen the note.
